wa_chianti_spire_east_face.descent_text: Same descent as the standard East Face/Rebel Yell line: rappel back down the route itself on fixed anchors rather than walking off. The usual descent is four double-rope rappels using two ropes (a single 60m may work for some stations but isn't the norm), starting from the summit block, then anchors near the top of pitch 5, then continuing stations down the route generally trending climber's-right. Anchors are fixed but should be visually checked each time — this isn't a heavily-bolted sport-style descent. Rope-snag hazard exists in the chimney/offwidth pitches. After reaching the base, reverse the Silver Star Glacier traverse and snow step back to Burgundy Col, then descend the climber's trail to Early Winters Creek and the highway — parties describe this exit as notably long and tiring relative to the climb, so plan daylight accordingly.

wa_east_face.descent_text: After summiting, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors. Make one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then a second, loose and dirty one into the moat at the base of the notch. Navigate the crevasse field on Chickamin Glacier to return to base camp.

wa_east_face_2.descent_text: From the summit area, downclimb via loose blocks and corners to locate the large granite horn with established sling anchor. This is a critical waypoint. Thread both 60m ropes through the horn slings. First double-rope rappel descends to the large slung horn at the top of pitch 2. Reanchor ropes there for the second rappel to complete descent to scree base of East Face. Exercise caution for rockfall and loose rock throughout the descent process.

wa_garfield_mountain_leaning_spire_west_.descent_text: Descend the line of ascent. A single 70 m rope handles it (60 m would probably work) via five or more rappels off trees and horns, linked by long stretches of downscrambling in the gully. Rappelling off the overhang near the summit into Gully #2 has been done, but getting out to that rappel is described as quite scary and it is not recommended. Below the Y Notch you are back on the Main Peak's South Route descent — a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, then the slab (two double-rope rappels if you rope it) and the dirt gully. Loose rock is the constant theme; the descent is where parties get hurt.

wa_jack_mountain_south_face.descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the southeast ridge back to the top of the south face, then pick a descent line of gray rock ribs and gully rather than the loose 'bowling alley' gully used on the way up — marker ducks placed on the ascent are commonly used to relocate the correct line. The crux is getting back down through the cliff band via the hidden chimney and Class 4 step; the majority of parties downclimb this face-to-face, belaying weaker members through the chimney and avoiding rappels because of loose, debris-prone rock that can be kicked onto climbers below. At least one party describes a rappel option through this same cliff band as the sketchiest rappel on the route, warning that a 30m rope leaves you short and forces a further downclimb — so if you do rappel here, bring at least a 45m single rope (a 60m rope, or a double-rope rappel with two shorter ropes, gives real margin). Any anchor here is natural — a sling around a boulder or horn (the same 'slinged boulder' landmark used on the approach) rather than any fixed/bolted gear — so bring cord/webbing and rap rings to build or back up the anchor. From the base of the cliff band, continue down scree and dirt slopes back to the Crater Creek Meadows camp (roughly 4 hours from the summit), then reverse the full approach: back over the 6,520ft notch, across (or high above) the Jerry Glacier, over the Crater Mountain saddle, and down FST 746/738 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead. Some parties use an alternate descent via Jerry Lakes, Devil's Lake, and the East Crater Mountain lookout, dropping via a ledge system below the glacier to avoid crossing the Jerry Glacier entirely (about 6.6 hours back to the vehicle from the lakes area). Key descent hazards: significant rockfall/loose-rock risk on the downclimb (helmets essential, stagger climbers, avoid kicking debris on parties below), crevasse hazard re-crossing the glacier, and route-finding difficulty in whiteout or late-day conditions given how long and complex this descent is.

wa_lexington_tower_east_face.descent_text: The standard descent is a walk-off, not a rappel-the-face descent. From the notch below the true summit (not the summit itself), head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left — roughly 20 feet of 3rd-class terrain. Old rap slings are present in this gully but most parties simply downclimb rather than bother rigging a rappel. From the base of the gully, traverse right (north) until you intersect the well-worn climbers'/cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to join the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road-walking versus following Blue Lake Trail all the way to its own trailhead. Some parties instead choose to rappel directly back down the East Face route itself (useful in bad weather or if the walk-off is unfamiliar/snow-covered) — one documented descent of the face took 7 double-rope (60m) rappels, built from a mix of slung horns/rap rings and a couple of fixed/bolted anchors encountered on route. That face-rappel line is not the recommended standard descent, just an alternative to the normal walk-off descent.

wa_liberty_bell_beckey_route.descent_text: This is the standard descent line for most Liberty Bell summit routes, not just the Beckey Route itself. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed.

wa_liberty_bell_overexposure.descent_text: The route’s 2nd pitch tops out at the same bolted anchor system that starts the standard Liberty Bell descent, so most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of 4th/low-5th-class scrambling to the true summit, then descend the standard way. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed. Some parties instead rappel back down the Overexposure line itself, a couple of enjoyable rappels on a mix of bolts and gear or tree anchors, directly into the approach couloir where packs were cached, particularly when the main descent line is congested.

wa_mount_olympus_blue_glacier.descent_text: Descend the same North Ridge/Blue Glacier line in reverse. From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock, the roughly Class 4 with one Class 5 (5.4-ish) step is reversed by rappel rather than downclimbed by most parties: build/clip the fixed summit anchor (recent parties note slung horns/blocks and a semi-permanent thin rappel line has appeared in some seasons, though this should not be trusted blindly) and rappel the north side of the summit block. A single-strand rappel with a 40-50m rope reaches the notch/belay ledge for most of the season; a 60m rope (doubled, ~30m per strand) is the safer bet as summer progresses and snow recedes below the block, and some parties join two ropes to make one long rappel to the base of the block instead of two shorter ones. An alternative is a single-rope rappel off the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then downclimbing the original route. Anchor material is a mix of fixed slings on horns/chockstones and natural gear (small cams in the 0.3-0.4 range have been used to back up or build anchors) rather than bolts — inspect any in-place tat before trusting it. Below the summit block, reverse the snow slope (mind the runout) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the Blue Glacier crossing, regain the lateral moraine catwalk, and retrace the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles back to the trailhead, watching for the ladder/washout section and any lingering steep snow between Glacier Meadows and Elk Lake.

wa_mount_thomson_west_ridge.descent_text: From the true summit, the standard descent follows the East Ridge back toward Bumblebee Pass rather than reversing the West Ridge climb. Walk/scramble off the east end of the summit block on a faint climbers' path to a notch where several parties over the years have left fixed tree anchors (webbing and rap rings, not bolts) at three points along the ridge's steeper steps — roughly around 6,200 ft and lower. Descent style varies by party and conditions: some downclimb the entire East Ridge unroped (sustained, exposed class 3–4 with a couple of low-5th moves), while most rope up for at least one section. A common approach is a single double-rope rappel (60m rope, doubled) off the initial tree anchor to bypass the steepest, most exposed step, then class 3 scrambling the rest of the way down; other parties describe using two to three shorter rappels off successive tree stations (doubled 8mm/thin rope, ~30m per rap) where the rock is loose or holds are wet, downclimbing the easier sections between them. Inspect any tat/rap rings before weighting them and back them up or replace old webbing if in doubt — these are climber-maintained natural anchors, not resupplied by any agency. Once off the ridge's technical ground, descend talus back into Bumblebee Basin, regain the steep boot path up and over Bumblebee Pass, drop back to the PCT near Ridge Lake, and retrace the Kendall Katwalk and switchbacks south to the PCT North Trailhead.

wa_olympus_summit_block_north_face.descent_text: The North Face Direct Finish climbs straight up the ~80 ft north face on generally solid rock (5.4, one pitch) rather than the standard east-face ramp system — enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rap anchor has built up at the top: a boulder/horn rigged with slings, a rap ring, and a quick link (inspect and back up any fixed tat, it is not agency-maintained). The rappel is roughly 80 to 100 ft from the summit down to the snow at the block's base — which a 60 m rope doubled (30 m/strand) reaches with room to spare. Bring a full 60 m rope, or plan to link two 30 m ropes, or use the lower intermediate station some parties have rigged to split it into two shorter rappels if carrying a shorter (30–40 m) rope. This single double-rope rappel lands you back on the snow essentially at the base of this finish. From there, reverse Crystal Pass, Snow Dome, the Blue Glacier and lateral moraine, and the Hoh River Trail back to the trailhead, typically with another night at Lewis Meadow or Elk Lake.

wa_the_scoop_2.descent_text: Parties who top out can use CBR's standard descent shared with the West Face: a single 30 m rappel east from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak to the base. The alternative, which avoids that loose ground, is to rappel the route itself: with two 60m ropes tied together, descend via a sequence of natural anchors — slung trees and horns down the crack systems below Launch Ledge — there are no bolts or fixed gear anywhere on the route, by design, so you are relying entirely on what you find or build (extra slings/cord are worth carrying). Watch for rope-snag risk in the corner systems on the crux Scoop pitch and loose rock low in the gully system if you bail before topping out. No count of rappels down the route itself is published; the route is about 1,000 ft over 10 pitches, so expect a long series, and be ready to build or equalize a natural anchor if a station looks marginal.

wa_the_tempest.descent_text: The Tempest was originally aided by its first ascensionists and later freed ground-to-summit; most parties who top out on the summit ridge use the standard Colchuck Balanced Rock walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the right (south) side of the true summit block to a broad sandy/scree gully, with a short step near the top sometimes eased by a single ~30m (100ft) rappel to the east off a sling around a horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — many parties simply downclimb this step instead. From there it's a loose scree/talus descent, clockwise around the peak, back to the base of the route (45 min-1hr). Parties who don't want the loose summit scramble — or who are bailing partway — instead rappel the route itself, tree-to-tree on natural anchors; the route can also be rappelled with two 60m ropes, avoiding the loose walk-off. Over the route's ~9 pitches (roughly 1,000+ ft) that works out to somewhere around 7-9 tree-anchor rappels with double 60m ropes. Watch for rope-snag risk in trees and loose blocks on this alpine wall either way.

wa_the_tiger.descent_text: Descend via double-rope rappels down the line of The Tiger using 70m ropes; alternatively, traverse across to the Ellen Pea route line for a rappel descent, or walk off via the 3rd-class ledge system to the west/summit ridge.
